varieties.name: Nonpareil
varieties.notes: The leading California almond, with flat kernels of excellent quality; ripens late August there.

varieties.name: Mission
varieties.notes: Also sold as Texas. Ripens 40 to 60 days after Nonpareil, with a hard shell and strongly flavored kernels.

varieties.name: All-in-One
varieties.notes: Paper-shelled and sweet; sold as hardy to zone 5, partly dwarfing, and self-fruitful.

crops.notes: Not self-fruitful; plant a second almond variety, or a peach that blooms at the same time. It blooms very early, and frost below about -2 °C during or after bloom kills the flowers, so it suits warm, low sites with mild springs and needs 400 to 500 hours below 7 °C in winter. Values from Utah State, University of California, and Oregon State guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12.

named.name: Bud 9 (B.9)
named.notes: Very winter hardy (zone 4), with the least spring-frost bud loss in Virginia Tech trials. Prone to collar rot and replant disease, so plant it on well-drained, fresh ground.

named.name: M.9
named.notes: Brittle roots, so stake it for life; extremely sensitive to fire blight. Occasionally winter injured in Kentucky, and among the least cold hardy in Cornell and Virginia Tech trials.

named.name: G.41
named.notes: Winter hardy; tolerates fire blight, collar rot, woolly apple aphid, and replant disease. Needs irrigation on light soils.

named.name: G.11
named.notes: Between M.9 and M.26 in size; winter hardy (zone 4 to 5) and resists fire blight and collar rot, but not woolly apple aphid.

named.name: G.16
named.notes: Like M.9 in size, with better anchorage; resists fire blight and collar rot. Use only virus-free scion wood.

named.name: M.26
named.notes: Very winter hardy, but very prone to fire blight and collar rot, and grows burr knots. Kentucky and New Hampshire advise a stake for life.

named.name: G.935
named.notes: Slightly larger than M.26 and very productive; resists fire blight and collar rot but not woolly apple aphid. Cornell found it loses winter hardiness early.

named.name: Bud 10 (B.10)
named.notes: Cold hardy and well anchored; tolerates fire blight.

named.name: G.202
named.notes: Resists fire blight, collar rot, and woolly apple aphid.

named.name: G.30
named.notes: Very winter hardy and better anchored than M.7, but the graft union is weak in early years with some varieties; support depends on the site.

named.name: M.7
named.notes: Cold hardy and tolerates many soils, but not heavy clay; shallow roots and many suckers. Stake it for the first four or five years.

named.name: G.969
named.notes: Winter hardy, with few suckers or burr knots; tolerates fire blight, collar rot, and woolly apple aphid.

named.name: G.890
named.notes: Cold hardy and very productive; resists fire blight, collar rot, and woolly apple aphid.

named.name: MM.106
named.notes: Well anchored and productive, but prone to collar and root rot, so not for poorly drained soil, and to injury from early winter freezes.

named.name: MM.111
named.notes: Very cold hardy (zone 3 to 4) and the best semi-dwarf for heavy soil; tolerates drier soil and resists woolly apple aphid. Slow to come into bearing.

named.name: Bud 118 (B.118)
named.notes: Extremely winter hardy (zone 3), well anchored, and productive; suits spur-type varieties and poor soil.

named.name: Antonovka
named.notes: A hardy Russian seedling rootstock for full-size trees, rated to zone 3; the hardiest of the common apple rootstocks.

named.name: Seedling
named.notes: Grown from seed of a hardy variety (zone 3); excellent hardiness, anchorage, and soil tolerance.

crops.notes: The rootstock sets the final size, so check it when buying; the default spacing is for a semi-dwarf tree. Most apples need a second, different variety nearby that blooms at the same time. Trees start fruiting in two to five years.

varieties.name: Goldrich
varieties.notes: Winter hardy and among the latest to bloom, so it escapes more spring frosts.

varieties.name: Harglow
varieties.notes: Winter hardy and late blooming.

varieties.name: Harogem
varieties.notes: Does well on warmer sites in New Hampshire.

varieties.name: Moorpark
varieties.notes: An old winter-hardy, later-blooming variety.

crops.notes: Usually self-fruitful, but crops better with a second variety that blooms at the same time. It blooms very early, so spring frost often takes the crop even in zones where the tree is hardy; choose later-blooming varieties and a slope, not a frost pocket. Poor in wet or heavy soil. Values from Utah State and New Hampshire extension; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (stone fruit).

varieties.name: Viking
varieties.notes: Large, abundant fruit clusters and fall color.

varieties.name: Autumn Magic
varieties.notes: Compact, with large, abundant fruit clusters and fall color.

crops.notes: Black chokeberry, a native shrub that spreads to 2 to 3 m across, with tart, dark berries for juice and jam. Self-compatible, though a second variety can improve fruit set. Fruits best in full sun. Values from Illinois, Minnesota, and Oregon State guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (berries, bushes).

Fast and frost tolerant. Sow every two to three weeks for a steady supply, and cut leaves young; older leaves grow strong and bitter. Heat above about 27 °C and dry soil make it bolt, so light shade helps in summer. Values from Wisconsin, Utah State, Clemson, and Maryland extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

named.name: Calleryana (Pyrus calleryana)
named.notes: Good in California and the Southeast, but lacks winter hardiness in most colder areas.

named.name: Betulifolia (Pyrus betulifolia)
named.notes: Takes every Asian pear variety; vigorous and tolerates heavy, wet soil.

varieties.name: Hosui
varieties.notes: Large russet fruit of excellent quality; thin the fruit for size. Ripens mid to late August.

varieties.name: Kosui
varieties.notes: Small to medium, apple-shaped brown fruit; ripens mid to late August.

varieties.name: Shinseiki
varieties.notes: Also called New Century. Partly self-fruitful; sweet, yellow fruit ripens early to mid August.

varieties.name: Olympic
varieties.notes: Also called Korean Giant. Large, late, golden russet fruit.

crops.notes: Partly self-fruitful, but crops much better with two or more varieties planted together. About as winter hardy as Bosc pear, to roughly -29 °C, though less hardy than Bartlett. The crisp fruit has tender skin that bruises easily. European pear rootstocks such as OHxF 87 and 97 also take it and dwarf it somewhat. Values from University of California, North Carolina State, Georgia, and Penn State extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (pears).
Planted as dormant crowns in a trench, which is what transplant means here. A bed crops for 15 years or more. Do not harvest in the first year, and only briefly in the second, so the roots build up.

Leaves are ready to pick a few weeks after planting out. Pinch off flower buds to keep it leafy. Blackens at the first frost and sulks below about 10 °C. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).
Each seed is a cluster that sends up several seedlings; thin to one. The young leaves are good to eat too.

Scorzonera, a long black-skinned root grown like salsify. Needs deep, loose soil worked 45 to 60 cm down for straight roots, and even moisture. The guide says to sow as soon as the soil can be worked, so the window is that of salsify. Values from Utah State extension. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's root and tuber group values.

Canes fruit in their second year, then die back; cut them out after harvest. Thornless trailing types such as Triple Crown need a trellis. Rubus fruticosus names the wider blackberry group; garden blackberries are hybrids within it.

Needs acid soil, around pH 4.5 to 5.5; most garden soil must be amended or the plants grown in raised beds of acid mix. Shallow roots like mulch and steady moisture. Two different varieties crop better than one. Values are for northern highbush; rabbiteye and southern highbush suit warmer zones.

A late spring frost or a week of nights below about 10 °C makes young plants bolt once it warms, and heat while heads form loosens them, so a crop sown in summer to mature in cool fall weather is the easier one. Dwarf types can sit closer. Values from Minnesota, Maryland, and Washington State extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Bees work its blue flowers all summer. Sow in place; the taproot makes it hard to move. Self-sows freely. Days to maturity are days to first bloom. Soil temperature for sowing from the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture (OMAFRA) borage crop profile; a germination study at North Dakota State University found a 9 °C minimum.
Cut the main head while the buds are tight, before they show yellow; side shoots follow for weeks. Hot weather makes heads loose and quick to flower.
A long-season crop for a fall harvest; frost improves the flavor. Pick sprouts from the bottom of the stem up as they firm.

Welsh onion, grown for green scallions; it never forms a bulb. Pull it any time after it is about 15 cm tall, and sow every few weeks through spring and summer. Left in place it forms a perennial clump that can be divided. Values from Penn State, Oregon State, Colorado State, and University of California guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (green onions).
Compact plants that need no support and crop over a few weeks. Seed rots in cold, wet soil, so wait for it to warm.
Water evenly; heads split after a dry spell followed by heavy rain. Harvest when heads feel firm.

Pot marigold. Flowers best in cool weather and may stall in midsummer heat; cut back and it blooms again in fall. Days to maturity are days to first bloom. Soil temperature for sowing from UNH Extension, "How to grow calendula".
Sow where it will grow; carrots do not transplant. Keep the seedbed moist until seedlings appear, and thin to the in-row spacing. Grown as an annual; it flowers in its second year.
The fussiest of the cabbage family. Heat, drought, or a check in growth gives small, early heads. Fold the inner leaves over the head once it shows to keep it white.

Celery grown for its swollen base. Seed is tiny and slow, so start it indoors about ten weeks ahead. It needs steady moisture and a long cool season; dig the roots in fall at about 8 to 10 cm across. Values from Washington State and Penn State extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).
Needs steady moisture and rich soil. Seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface. Plant out after nights warm up; a long cold spell can make it bolt.

German (annual) chamomile, picked for tea as the flowers open fully. Seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface. Thrives in poor, well-drained soil and self-sows freely. Values from Wisconsin, University of California, and Texas A&M guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Cut leaves to a few centimetres above the soil and they regrow all season. Divide clumps every few years. The flowers are edible too. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's green onion values, with the small-vegetable initial value; FAO-56 does not list chives.

Bolts quickly in heat, so sow small batches every few weeks in spring and again in fall. The seeds are coriander. Does not like being transplanted. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Seed comes up slowly in cold spring soil, so start spring plants indoors and sow in place in late summer for fall. Pick the lower leaves and the plant keeps growing; it stands through frost and light freezes. Values from Clemson and Penn State extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Grown for its leaves, which are rich in potassium and break down fast, as a mulch, compost material, or soaked into a liquid feed; bumblebees work the flowers. Most gardeners plant Russian comfrey 'Bocking 14' (Symphytum × uplandicum), which sets no seed, from root cuttings. Any piece of root left in the ground regrows, so choose a permanent spot. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which harm the liver; do not eat it or drink it as tea.
Spacing assumes plants grown up a trellis; allow about twice as much in-row space when they sprawl. Dislikes root disturbance, so start indoors in individual pots.

Sow where it will grow; it dislikes transplanting. Leaves are ready in about six weeks and seed heads later in summer. Left to flower, it self-seeds. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list dill or other herbs.

Vegetable soybean, picked while the pods are plump and still green. Bushes stand 35 to 60 cm and need no support. Plants flower as days shorten, so sowing one variety again later does not spread the harvest; sow early and late varieties together instead. Values from Utah State and Penn State extension guides.
Needs more heat than tomatoes or peppers. Plant out only once nights stay warm; a cold spell stunts plants for weeks.

varieties.name: Wyldewood
varieties.notes: Selected in Missouri; fairly tolerant of alkaline soil, with large clusters of medium to large berries.

varieties.name: Adams 2
varieties.notes: Tolerates alkaline soil; medium berries in large clusters.

varieties.name: York
varieties.notes: An older variety with the largest berries of the American kinds; ripens early.

crops.notes: American elderberry, a large shrub 2 to 2.5 m tall and wide. Only partly self-fruitful, so plant two varieties for good crops. Tolerates some shade but fruits best in full sun; prune every year. In zone 3 it survives but may not ripen. Values from Utah State, Minnesota, and Wisconsin extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (berries, bushes).

Curly endive and broad-leaved escarole, grown like lettuce but more bitter; tying the outer leaves over the heart for a week or two before harvest blanches it milder. Values from Washington State and Penn State extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Broad bean, a cool-season crop grown like peas rather than like warm-season beans; plants take frost down to about -7 to -9 °C and grow 60 to 120 cm tall. The guides say to sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, so the window here is pea's. Where winters are mild it is also sown in fall to overwinter. Values from Oregon State and University of California guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (fresh faba bean).

varieties.name: Celeste
varieties.notes: Fairly hardy; small violet-brown fruit with pink pulp, ripening from mid-July in North Carolina.

varieties.name: Brown Turkey
varieties.notes: Also sold as Texas Everbearing. Medium to large coppery fruit; regrows and fruits on suckers after a freeze.

varieties.name: Brunswick
varieties.notes: Also called Magnolia. Large fruit that splits in hot, humid weather, so best for preserves; fairly cold hardy.

crops.notes: Grown as a bush or small tree. Choose a variety that sets fruit without pollination, such as Celeste, Brown Turkey, or Marseilles. Temperatures near -18 °C kill parts of the plant, so give it a sunny, sheltered spot; it starts bearing in about five or six years. Values from North Carolina State, Georgia, and Oregon State guides.

The bulbing fennel, not the seed fennel grown as an herb. Keep the soil evenly moist; drought, root damage, long days, and heat make it bolt, so pick a slow-bolting variety and time it to mature in cool weather. Sow a short row every three to four weeks for a steady supply. Values from Utah State extension. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list fennel.

Flat, mildly garlic-flavored leaves and white late-summer flowers. It self-sows heavily and can spread, so cut the flower heads before they set seed. Clumps can be divided in early spring. The guides give no frost-anchored dates, so the windows are those of chives. Values from Wisconsin, New Hampshire, and Clemson extension guides.

Grown from cloves planted in fall, pointed end up, and harvested the next summer when the lower leaves turn brown. Grown as an annual crop. Hardneck types such as Music suit cold winters; softneck types suit mild ones.

varieties.name: Poorman
varieties.notes: An American type, very productive and very cold hardy, with medium red fruit; resists powdery mildew.

varieties.name: Hinnomaki Red
varieties.notes: Sweet berries with tart skins; resists powdery mildew and may fruit the year it is planted.

varieties.name: Invicta
varieties.notes: A European type with heavy crops of large green berries on very spiny bushes; resists powdery mildew.

varieties.name: Captivator
varieties.notes: Large, sweet, reddish fruit on tall bushes with few spines; resists powdery mildew.

crops.notes: A thorny bush 1 to 1.5 m tall and wide; self-fertile, so one plant bears. Needs at least 1,000 hours of winter chill and does best with some shade in the hottest part of the day. Fruits on one-year-old wood and older spurs. Values from Utah State and Minnesota extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (berries, bushes).

American and cold-hardy hybrid grapes for eating, juice, and wine; hardiness depends on the variety, from Marquette and Bluebell (zone 3 to 4) to Concord (zone 5). American varieties are the hardiest and most disease resistant; European wine grapes need milder winters. Needs a trellis and pruning every year. Values from Illinois, Minnesota, Oregon State, and Penn State guides and the Fedco Trees catalog (2026); crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (table grapes).

Kiwiberry, a vigorous vine up to 12 m long with smooth, grape-sized fruit. Plants are male or female, so plant a male within about 12 m of the females; only Issai sets some fruit alone. Needs a sturdy trellis. Hardy to about -23 to -32 °C, but late spring frost can kill new shoots. Values from Utah State and Oregon State extension and the Fedco Trees catalog (2026); crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (kiwi).

varieties.name: Tundra
varieties.notes: Firm, fairly large fruit; resists powdery mildew.

varieties.name: Borealis
varieties.notes: About 1.2 m tall, with large, very good-tasting fruit; suits a home garden.

varieties.name: Indigo Gem
varieties.notes: Heavy crops of smaller, tangier fruit; somewhat prone to powdery mildew.

crops.notes: Honeyberry, an extremely hardy shrub up to 1.8 m that lives about 30 years and ripens blue berries early in summer. Needs an unrelated variety that blooms at the same time for pollination. Above zone 6 it suffers leaf scorch, mildew, and early leaf drop. Values from Utah State extension; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (berries, bushes).

American hazelnut and its hybrids, hardy to zone 3 or 4; European filberts are less hardy. Every hazelnut needs another to pollinate it, so plant two or three within about 15 m. Starts bearing in about five or six years. Usually kept as a shrub about 4.5 m tall and 3 m wide; in orchards space plants 4.5 to 6 m apart. Values from Utah State and Oregon State guides.
Grown like sweet pepper but likes it warmer; seeds sprout slowly in cool soil. Fruit grows hotter as it ripens, and dry spells at fruiting raise the heat further.

Pick the outer leaves and let the centre keep growing. Light frost sweetens the leaves, and plants often crop into winter. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Grown for its swollen stem; pick it at 5 to 8 cm across, before it turns woody. A week or more of nights below about 10 °C can make young plants bolt, and summer heat makes the stems tough, so grow it in spring or fall. Values from Utah State, Minnesota, and Colorado State extension guides. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list kohlrabi.

English lavender. Usually started from cuttings, since seed is slow and takes months to reach planting size. Needs sharp drainage and little water or fertilizer; wet soil rots the roots, and rich feeding gives leaves over flowers. Fall planting works only with about two months of mild weather before winter. Values from Utah State and Florida extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Plant seedlings deep, or mound soil around the stems as they grow, to get long white shanks. Stands in the ground through frost for a late harvest. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list leek.

A lemon-scented mint relative that forms large clumps and grows in sun or part shade. It self-sows freely, so cut off the flowers; cutting hard after flowering also brings fresh leaves. Seed is slow to germinate. Values from Wisconsin and Clemson extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

A tender grass grown from divisions or rooted stalks, planted out once frost has passed; it grows slowly until summer heat, then up to 1 to 2 m tall and about 1 m wide with plenty of water. Outside zones 9 and 10, grow it in a pot or keep a rooted piece of the stalk base indoors over winter. Values from Utah State and Clemson extension guides.
A cool-season crop that bolts in summer heat. Sow small batches every two to three weeks; part shade helps in hot climates. Seed needs light to germinate, so cover it only lightly.

Needs warmer soil and a longer, hotter season than snap beans, and prefers sandier soil; in cool summers it yields poorly. Bush types mature first; pole types take longer and need support. Cook before eating, as raw beans can carry small amounts of toxic glucosides. Values from Minnesota, Colorado State, Penn State, and Maine extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

A tall celery-flavored perennial, 90 to 120 cm, for rich, fairly moist soil; light shade helps in hot summers. Seed is sown in late summer, and young plants or divisions are set out in early spring; the window is that of chives, since the guides give no frost-anchored date. Zones come from seed-company guides (Johnny's Seeds), as extension guides give none. Values from Maryland, Illinois, and Missouri extension guides.
French marigold, the kind used in the companion trials. Days to maturity are days to first bloom. Frost kills it.
Milder than oregano. A tender perennial grown as an annual outside mild winters; it grows 15 to 30 cm tall and does well in pots. Values from Clemson, Missouri, and Texas A&M extension guides.
Includes cantaloupe and honeydew. Needs a long, hot season; black plastic mulch helps in cool areas. Water less as fruit ripens for sweeter melons; cantaloupes are ripe when they slip from the vine.
Spreads fast by underground runners; grow it in a container or a pot sunk in the bed. Usually planted from divisions or nursery plants, since it does not come true from seed. Tolerates part shade.

Young plants shrug off light frost, though a hard freeze can injure them. Heat above about 24 °C slows growth and brings on bolting, so the fall crop, maturing in cool weather, is usually the better one. The spacing is for picking young leaves; give plants grown to full size 20 to 45 cm. Values from Utah State, Clemson, Maryland, and Washington State extension guides. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list mustard greens.

Chinese cabbage with tall, tight heads. A late frost or a week of nights below about 10 °C makes spring plants bolt, and heat as heads form loosens them, so a crop sown in midsummer to head in cool fall weather is the more reliable one. Values from Minnesota, Maryland, Penn State, and Washington State extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).
Sow where it is to grow; it resents transplanting. Rich soil gives leaves instead of flowers. Leaves and flowers are edible. Days to maturity are days to first bloom.

named.name: Guardian
named.notes: Preferred in the Southeast for tolerance of peach tree short life.

named.name: Lovell
named.notes: The long-standing reference peach rootstock, also used for nectarines.

crops.notes: A smooth-skinned peach, grown the same way; self-fruitful. Like peach it blooms early, so spring frost can take the crop, and it is prone to brown rot and blight. Prune every year to an open centre. Values from Oregon State, Alabama, and Penn State extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (stone fruit).

A hot-weather crop. Soak seed overnight before sowing. Pick pods small and every day or two; they toughen quickly. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Bulbs form in response to day length, so choose a type for your latitude. Short-day onions suit mild-winter regions; long-day onions suit the north. Direct sowing here means planting sets (small bulbs), 2–3 cm deep.

Flavor is strongest in lean, well-drained soil and full sun. Seed needs light to germinate, so press it onto the surface. Cut back after flowering. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Very slow to germinate; soaking seed overnight helps. Grows in part shade. It flowers and turns bitter in its second year, so most gardeners sow it fresh each year. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Use fresh seed each year; it loses vigour fast and is slow to come up. Leave roots in the ground until after a few frosts for the sweetest flavor. The sap can irritate skin in sunlight, so wear gloves when handling the leaves.

varieties.name: Sunflower
varieties.notes: Among the highest-yielding in north Alabama trials.

varieties.name: Overleese
varieties.notes: An older named variety grown in Alabama trials.

varieties.name: Shenandoah
varieties.notes: One of the Peterson pawpaw varieties.

varieties.name: KSU-Atwood
varieties.notes: A Kentucky State University release.

crops.notes: A native understory tree up to about 9 m in full sun. Not self-pollinating, so plant two unrelated trees within about 9 m of each other; hand pollination helps where pollinators are scarce. Young own-root plants need shade to establish, and it suckers into a patch. Grafted trees bear in a few years, seedlings in up to 10. Values from Clemson, Maryland, Penn State, Illinois, Missouri, Alabama, and North Carolina State guides.
A cool-season crop sown as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it stops cropping in summer heat. Most types climb and need netting or twiggy supports.

named.name: MP-29
named.notes: Semi-dwarf, about 40 to 75 percent the size of trees on Guardian depending on site; resists peach tree short life and Armillaria root rot.

named.name: Lovell
named.notes: The long-standing reference rootstock, with good anchorage, high survival in northern trials, and more cold hardiness than Nemaguard, but suffers in waterlogged soil.

named.name: Bailey
named.notes: Recommended in Ontario; gives uniform medium to large trees, lends some cold hardiness to the variety, and survives severe winters well. Slightly dwarfing.

named.name: Guardian
named.notes: Preferred in the Southeast for tolerance of peach tree short life.

named.name: Krymsk 86
named.notes: Hardy to USDA zone 4 with excellent anchorage, and tolerates wet soil; prone to bacterial canker in the Southeast.

named.name: Halford
named.notes: An older, vigorous rootstock.

named.name: Nemaguard
named.notes: Needs well-drained soil, as it is very susceptible to wet feet, and is less cold hardy than Lovell; best only where stone fruit has not been grown before.

crops.notes: Self-fertile, so one tree is enough. It blooms early, and a late spring frost can take the crop even where the tree itself is hardy; plant on a slope rather than in a frost pocket. Fruits on last year's wood, so prune every year to an open centre.

Needs a frost-free season of at least 110 to 130 days. After flowering the pegs push into the soil, so hill soil around plants once they are about 30 cm tall and keep it loose and evenly moist. Dig before frost and dry the plants for a week or two before picking the pods. Values from Utah State and Penn State extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (groundnut).

named.name: Pyrodwarf
named.notes: Winter hardy, very precocious, and highly tolerant of fire blight; does not sucker.

named.name: Quince
named.notes: The European dwarfing root, but not recommended in the U.S. as it is sensitive to cold; very prone to fire blight, and Bartlett and Bosc are incompatible with it.

named.name: OHxF 333
named.notes: Winter hardy and well anchored, replacing quince; resists fire blight, collar rot, and woolly aphid.

named.name: Pyro 222
named.notes: Precocious and productive; tolerates a wide range of soils.

named.name: OHxF 87
named.notes: The most precocious Old Home x Farmingdale; winter hardy, well anchored, does not sucker, and resists fire blight.

named.name: OHxF 40
named.notes: About two-thirds of standard size; resists fire blight, crown rot, and pear decline.

named.name: Seedling
named.notes: Bartlett seedlings are the standard; winter hardy and very productive, but tree size varies.

named.name: OHxF 97
named.notes: Vigorous, near seedling size but more uniform; winter hardy (zone 3 to 4) and well anchored, resists fire blight, and suits Asian pears.

named.name: Calleryana (Pyrus calleryana)
named.notes: Preferred in the Southeast for European and Asian pears.

named.name: Betulifolia (Pyrus betulifolia)
named.notes: Vigorous and tolerates heavy, wet soil; suits Asian pears, but is less winter hardy than other pear rootstocks. Sources differ on its fire blight tolerance.

crops.notes: Needs a second variety nearby for pollination. Pick European pears mature but still firm and let them ripen indoors; tree-ripened pears turn gritty at the core. Starts fruiting in three to six years.

varieties.name: Prok
varieties.notes: Grafted and self-pollinating, with large crops of sweet fruit from mid-September.

varieties.name: Yates
varieties.notes: Grafted and self-pollinating; fast-growing, with sweet fruit ripening in early September.

crops.notes: A native fruit tree hardy to zone 5. Sources differ on pollination; some named varieties bear alone, but planting two trees gives the most reliable crop. Fruit ripens late in fall and is astringent until fully soft. Asian persimmons are less hardy, surviving only to about -12 °C. Values from Illinois, Oregon State, Penn State, Missouri, North Carolina State, and Mississippi State guides.

named.name: Lovell (peach)
named.notes: The preferred rootstock for European plums in Alabama.

named.name: Myrobalan
named.notes: A plum seedling rootstock for European plums, hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Stanley
varieties.notes: A European plum that grows well in New Hampshire.

varieties.name: Early Italian
varieties.notes: A European plum that grows well in New Hampshire.

varieties.name: Green Gage
varieties.notes: A European plum that grows well in New Hampshire.

varieties.name: Castleton
varieties.notes: A European plum that grows well in New Hampshire.

crops.notes: European plum. Many are self-fruitful but bear more with a second European variety nearby. Japanese plums (zones 5 to 9) need a Japanese or American plum to pollinate them, as European plum pollen does not work. Poor in wet or heavy soil. Values from Utah State, Alabama, and New Hampshire extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (stone fruit).
Climbing vines that need a pole, trellis, or teepee about 2 m tall. Slower to start than bush beans but keep cropping until frost if picked often.

Grown from seed potatoes (tubers or pieces with eyes), not seed. Mound soil over the stems as they grow so tubers stay covered and green-free. Frost kills the leaves, but the tubers underground survive a light frost.
Needs a lot of room. Count back from your first frost so fruit ripens in time; harvest when the skin is hard and the stem starts to dry.

A heading chicory with bitter red leaves. Young plants take frost down to about -7 °C, but heat above about 24 °C makes it bolt and turn bitter, so it does best maturing in cool weather. Sow a few seeds for each plant, as germination is uneven. Grown as an annual, though chicory is a perennial. Values from Utah State and Washington State extension guides. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list radicchio.
Fast and easy. Sow a short row every week or two; roots turn woody and hot if left in the ground or grown in summer heat.

Planted as dormant canes. Summer-bearing types fruit on last year's canes; fall-bearing types such as Heritage fruit on this year's and can be cut to the ground each winter. A wire or trellis keeps rows upright. Suckers spread, so keep a mown path around the row.

varieties.name: Red Lake
varieties.notes: Widely available and vigorous, with large, bright red berries; prone to powdery mildew.

varieties.name: Rovada
varieties.notes: Large berries in long clusters; flowers late, so it misses frosts, and resists powdery mildew.

varieties.name: Honeyqueen
varieties.notes: A long harvest of tender, juicy fruit; resists powdery mildew.

crops.notes: A bush 1 to 1.5 m tall that stays productive for 20 years; self-fertile. Grows best with morning sun and afternoon shade and good air flow; heat above about 29 °C and strong sun scorch the leaves. Blooms very early, so avoid frost pockets. Values from Utah State and Minnesota extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (berries, bushes).

Planted as crowns, with the buds just below the surface. Eat only the stalks; the leaves are poisonous. Skip harvest the first year, then pull stalks in spring and early summer. Needs a cold winter to do well. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's values for perennial vegetables with winter dormancy; FAO-56 does not list rhubarb.

An evergreen shrub, grown from cuttings because seed is slow and unreliable. Outside zones 8 to 10 grow it in a pot and bring it in before frost; a few varieties such as Arp take zone 7 with shelter. Wet soil and overwatering cause root rot. Values from Penn State, Illinois, and Texas A&M extension guides. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Slower than turnip and sweetest when the roots fill out in cool fall weather, so it is mostly sown in summer to mature a few weeks after the first frost; a spring crop works only where summers stay cool. Pull roots at about 10 cm across. Values from Utah State and Clemson extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12.

A woody, short-lived perennial; replace plants every few years as they turn leggy. Needs excellent drainage and tolerates drought. Cut it back in spring and through summer for fresh shoots, never more than half the plant at once. Days to maturity are to the first harvest. Values from Wisconsin, Clemson, Missouri, and Texas A&M extension guides.

A long, slender root with an oyster-like flavor, sown in place in spring and dug in fall; frost improves it, and roots can stay in the ground into winter. Needs deep, loose soil. Values from Maryland, Penn State, and Washington State extension guides. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's root and tuber group values; FAO-56 does not list salsify.

Usually planted as bulb sets, 2.5 to 5 cm deep. Close spacing gives single bulbs, wider spacing clusters of up to a dozen. Lift when the tops fall over, and stop feeding by midsummer so the bulbs store. Plant in early spring or, where winters allow, in fall. Values from Utah State, Washington State, and Maryland extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (dry onions).

named.name: Mahaleb
named.notes: The usual rootstock for standard sour cherries; Gisela semi-dwarfs are becoming common.

varieties.name: Montmorency

varieties.name: North Star
varieties.notes: Naturally dwarf, so it suits a home orchard.

varieties.name: Meteor

crops.notes: Tart or pie cherry, such as Montmorency. Self-fruitful, so one tree is enough, and hardier than sweet cherry. Sweet and sour cherries cannot pollinate each other. Compact varieties such as North Star stay near 3 m. Values from Penn State, Oregon State, Illinois, Minnesota, and New Hampshire extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12 (cherries).
A cool-season crop that bolts as days lengthen and warm. Sow again in late summer for a fall crop.

The sweetleaf herb. It does not take frost and barely grows below about 15 °C, so set plants out after the last frost once nights stay above about 10 °C, and pinch the tips for bushier plants. Outside zones 9 to 11 grow it as an annual or bring it indoors. Zones and spacing from seed-company guides (Johnny's Seeds), as extension guides give none. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Planted as bare-root crowns, with the crown level with the soil. June-bearing types fruit once a year from the second season; remove their first-year flowers. Day-neutral types such as Albion fruit through summer from the first year. Replant every three or four years as yields fall.
Bush-type plants, including zucchini. Pick fruit young and often; one or two plants feed most households.

Sow on the surface; the seed needs light. Its small flowers feed hoverflies, whose larvae eat aphids. A favorite host of Bagrada bug, so skip it where that pest is building up. Days to maturity are days to first bloom.

named.name: Gisela 3
named.notes: The most dwarfing Gisela; only for the best soils, with fair anchorage. USDA zone 5.

named.name: Gisela 5
named.notes: Needs well-drained soil and does poorly in heavy soil; fair to good anchorage, and trees lean away from strong wind.

named.name: Gisela 12
named.notes: Very winter hardy (to about -29 °C), precocious, and adapts to a wide range of soils.

named.name: Gisela 6
named.notes: Tolerates heavier soil; very productive, so West Virginia advises support. Smaller in the eastern U.S. than in the Pacific Northwest.

named.name: Krymsk 6
named.notes: Winter hardy (USDA zone 5) and heat tolerant, with good anchorage; needs good drainage.

named.name: Krymsk 5
named.notes: Winter hardy (USDA zone 5), with good anchorage; tolerates heavy, wet soil and drought better than the Gisela rootstocks.

named.name: Mazzard
named.notes: Winter hardy (zone 4), with good anchorage and wide soil tolerance given good drainage; not precocious.

named.name: Mahaleb
named.notes: Slightly dwarfing, drought tolerant, and winter hardy, but very sensitive to waterlogged soil. Some newer varieties, such as Chelan and Tieton, are incompatible with it.

named.name: Colt
named.notes: Tolerates wet, heavy soil better than Mahaleb or Gisela 5, but is not winter hardy; semi-vigorous in Europe, full size in the Pacific Northwest.

crops.notes: Most sweet cherries need a pollination partner; Stella is self-fertile. Net trees as fruit colours, or birds take the crop. Sour cherries (Prunus cerasus) are hardier and self-fertile, and are a separate crop.
Wind-pollinated, so plant a block of several short rows rather than one long row. Keep supersweet types apart from other corn, and give them warmer soil.
Slow to germinate and needs warm soil. Plant out once nights stay above about 13 °C; cold nights stall growth.

Grown from slips (rooted sprouts) rather than seed; indoor start here means sprouting slips from a stored root. Needs warm soil and a long season. Too much nitrogen gives leaves instead of roots. Cure the roots somewhere warm for a week or two before storing.

Leafy beet relative grown for its leaves and stems. Pick outer leaves and it keeps producing from spring into fall; it tolerates more heat than spinach. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's small-vegetable group values; FAO-56 does not list chard.

Its flowers draw lacewings, lady beetles, parasitic wasps, and tachinid flies, which prey on aphids, whiteflies, and caterpillars. As a companion for potatoes it did not reduce Colorado potato beetle in field trials. Invasive in much of North America and a listed noxious weed in several states; check local rules. Toxic to people and livestock. Spreads by roots and seed, so grow it contained and cut flowers before they set seed.

A small woody subshrub. Needs sharp drainage and dislikes wet winters more than cold ones. Trim after flowering to keep it bushy; replace plants that turn woody after a few years. Crop coefficients from Pereira et al. (2024), Irrigation Science 42:1199–1228, doi:10.1007/s00271-024-00960-4 (CC BY 4.0).

Plant at least two, since one plant does not set fruit on its own. Sprawls and keeps fruiting until frost; a stake or cage keeps the husked fruit off the ground. Too much fertilizer gives leaves instead of fruit. Days to maturity are from transplanting. Values from Utah State extension. Crop coefficients are FAO-56 Table 12's values for the tomato family (Solanaceae); FAO-56 does not list tomatillo.
Frost kills it. Wait until nights stay above 10 °C before planting out.

Always sown in place. Pull roots at 5 to 7 cm across; the leaves are good as greens at any size, though picking many slows the root. Tastes best when it grows fast in cool weather; even moisture keeps roots from cracking or turning bitter. Values from Utah State, Clemson, Colorado State, and Penn State extension guides; crop coefficients from FAO-56 Table 12.

A perennial of stream banks, usually grown as an annual in gardens. Its soil must stay wet, so grow it at a water's edge or in a container standing in water that is changed often. Seed germinates best in cool, wet conditions; stem cuttings root quickly. Values from Utah State extension.
Needs heat and space; small "icebox" types such as Sugar Baby suit shorter seasons. Ripe when the spot resting on the ground turns creamy yellow and the nearest tendril dries.

Sprawling vines grown for storage. Winter squash covers several Cucurbita species; these values suit butternut types and are close for acorn and buttercup. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail, before frost, and cure in the sun for storage.

pests.signs: Soft, pear-shaped insects 2 to 4 mm long, green, black, red, yellow, brown, or grey, with two short tailpipes at the rear. They cluster under young leaves and on new shoots and buds, leave white cast skins, and drip sticky honeydew that grows black sooty mould. Heavy feeding twists and yellows leaves and stunts shoots, and aphids spread viruses such as cucumber mosaic.

cultural: Pull weeds that host aphids, such as sowthistle and wild mustard.
physical: Knock aphids off with a strong spray of water, which also rinses off honeydew.
biological: Lady beetles, lacewings, hoverfly larvae, and parasitic wasps eat aphids; give them time to catch up.
Grow flowers that bloom across the season to keep natural enemies near, and avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill them.

regions.when: Look under young leaves and on new shoots often all season; numbers can climb within days.
regions.threshold: Most aphid feeding does the plant little harm. Act only when leaves curl or yellow or shoots stunt.

organic: Insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or pyrethrins kill only the aphids they touch; spray both sides of the leaves and repeat.
Neem (azadirachtin) stops aphids feeding, and they die slowly.
conventional: Long-lasting broad-spectrum insecticides kill natural enemies too and can make aphids worse.

pests.signs: Tiny beetles, 1.5 to 3 mm long, black, bronze, bluish, or grey and sometimes striped, that jump when disturbed. They chew shallow pits and many small round holes, under 3 mm across, in the leaves. Heavy feeding wilts or stunts young plants; seedlings suffer more than transplants.

cultural: Control weeds near the garden and clear old crop debris, where adults spend the winter.
Plant late in the planting window, so warm weather makes plants grow past the damage quickly.
Sow a favoured crop such as radish a week or two before the main crop as a trap, and deal with the beetles on it.
physical: Cover seedlings with row cover, on hoops for eggplant, and take it off before flowering so pollinators can reach the flowers.
Kaolin clay on the leaves can deter feeding, with mixed results; reapply after rain.
biological: A native braconid wasp kills adult flea beetles, and lacewing larvae eat them; neither is sold.

regions.when: From the day seedlings come up or transplants go in, through spring. Yellow sticky cards show when they arrive, and beetles are slower and easier to see on cool mornings.
regions.threshold: Protect seedlings when there are more than five beetles per plant, or when 10 to 30 percent of their leaves are lost. Once plants have four or five leaves, usually by summer, they outgrow the damage.

organic: Spinosad or pyrethrins.
conventional: Broad-spectrum insecticides such as carbaryl, malathion, permethrin, lambda-cyhalothrin, or cyfluthrin.

pests.signs: Oval beetles about 1 cm long with an orange shield behind the head and cream wing covers with ten narrow black stripes. Clusters of bright yellow-orange eggs sit under the leaves. Larvae are brick red when young, then pink to salmon, with black heads and two rows of dark spots on each side. Larvae and adults chew the leaves and can strip a plant.

cultural: Pull nightshade and ground cherry near the garden, mulch between plants, and clean up at season's end.
Grow an early variety (under 80 days) to finish before midsummer adults build up.
Skip potatoes for a year; the beetles move little, so this works best with no other potatoes nearby.
physical: Hand-pick adults and larvae into soapy water and crush the egg clusters, starting as adults come out in spring.
Cover rows with row cover before any beetles appear, where potatoes did not grow last year; remove it when weather turns hot and humid.
biological: Lady beetles and stink bugs eat the eggs, though they seldom keep numbers down on their own.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Leptinotarsa decemlineata distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26); absent, eradicated, transient, or only intercepted elsewhere

regions.when: From when the potatoes come up in spring, as overwintered adults emerge; check regularly, as a second generation follows by midsummer in warmer areas.
regions.threshold: Potatoes can lose up to 30 percent of their leaves before flowering, but only about 10 percent once the tubers start to size, soon after flowering.

organic: Bt or neem on small larvae, before numbers are high.
Spinosad, though some populations resist it.
This beetle resists more than 50 insecticides; never rely on one product, and treat young larvae, not eggs or adults.

pests.signs: Flat, dark grey-brown bugs about 1.6 cm long with orange and brown stripes along the edge of the abdomen. Clusters of about 20 oval, yellow to bronze eggs sit under the leaves, often in the angle between veins. Nymphs start green with black legs and turn grey. Feeding makes yellow spots that turn brown, and heavy feeding wilts and can kill young plants. In fall they crowd onto the fruit.

cultural: Keep plants watered and fed, as sturdy plants tolerate feeding.
Clear plant debris during the season, and cucurbit vines in fall, where adults hide and spend the winter.
Butternut and buttercup squash and Sweet Cheese pumpkins tolerate feeding better than other kinds.
A border of Blue Hubbard squash draws squash bugs away from the main crop; deal with the bugs on it.
Where squash bugs are a steady problem, skip straw mulch, which shelters them.
physical: Crush the egg clusters, and drop nymphs and adults into soapy water.
Lay boards or newspaper on the ground; the bugs gather under them at night, to be destroyed in the morning.

regions.when: Adults reach cucurbits from late spring; look under the leaves for egg clusters from midsummer, as treatment works best on newly hatched nymphs.
regions.threshold: About one egg cluster per plant on average.

conventional: Seldom needed in a garden. Treat newly hatched nymphs and cover the leaf undersides, late in the day when the flowers have closed, to spare bees.

pests.signs: A day-flying, wasp-like moth about 1.3 cm long, with an orange abdomen dotted black and metallic green front wings. It lays flat brown eggs at the base of the plant, and cream larvae with brown heads, up to 2.5 cm long, bore into the stem. Plants wilt, first in strong sun and then by morning, and holes near the base ooze moist green or orange sawdust-like frass. The stem base can rot.

cultural: Grow crops it seldom attacks, such as butternut squash, cucumber, melon, and watermelon; Hubbard and acorn squash suffer most.
Rotate where cucurbits grow, and pull and destroy plants it kills.
physical: Cover plants with row cover, sealed at the edges, when vines start to run or the first moth is seen, until about two weeks after that first moth; remove it at flowering, and do not use it where cucurbits grew last year, as moths emerge from the soil underneath.
Slit a wilting stem lengthwise, kill the larvae, and mound moist soil over the cut so new roots can form.

regions.when: Moths fly from late June through July in Minnesota. Watch for them, set a yellow bowl of soapy water by late June and check it daily, and look closely at any plant wilted in the morning.

cultural: Sow a second summer squash in early July, which matures after the moths have finished laying.
organic: Bt does not work, as larvae inside the stem never eat it.
conventional: Spray or dust the stem bases when vines start to run or the first moth is seen, and repeat every 7 to 10 days through July, before larvae enter the stems; carbaryl, permethrin, bifenthrin, or esfenvalerate. Spray in the evening, not on open flowers.

pests.signs: A green caterpillar up to 10 cm long with eight white V-shaped marks on each side and a black horn at the tail; young ones are pale and unmarked. It strips leaves from the top of the plant down and chews holes in fruit, and leaves dark green or black droppings. It blends in and is often found only after much damage.

cultural: Pull weeds that host it, such as horsenettle, jimsonweed, and nightshade.
Till after harvest to destroy pupae in the soil.
physical: Hand-pick caterpillars into soapy water; it is the most effective control.
biological: Leave hornworms carrying white, rice-like cocoons; the parasitic wasps inside will kill them and go on to others.
Lady beetles, lacewings, and paper wasps eat the eggs and young caterpillars.

regions.when: At least twice a week in summer, looking for stripped tops and droppings; there are two generations a year.
regions.threshold: Hand-picking is usually enough. Treat only small caterpillars, before plants lose many leaves.

organic: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki) on small caterpillars, which spares bees and other insects, or insecticidal soap, which has little effect on beneficial insects.
Spinosad, which is toxic to bees until it dries.
conventional: Broad-spectrum pyrethroids such as bifenthrin or permethrin kill beneficial insects too.

pests.signs: Beetles about 5 mm long, yellow with three black stripes (striped) or with twelve black spots (spotted), with black heads. They chew leaves, flowers, and stems and scar fruit, and can strip small plants. The striped beetle carries bacterial wilt, which makes cucumbers and melons wilt and die.

cultural: Pull weeds near the garden and clear debris and leaf litter in fall, where adults spend the winter, and rotate.
Pull any plant with bacterial wilt before beetles spread it.
Plant Blue Hubbard squash a week or two before the other cucurbits as a trap, and deal with the beetles on it.
physical: Cover plants with row cover from emergence, and remove it at flowering so pollinators can reach them.
Thick straw at the base of plants makes egg-laying harder; knock beetles into soapy water on a few plants.
Kaolin clay deters feeding if applied before heavy damage.

regions.when: From when seedlings come up, watching closely from the seed leaves to the third true leaf; keep watching cucumbers and melons all season because of bacterial wilt. Beetles seen late in summer can be ignored.
regions.threshold: Treat seedlings when 25 percent of plants have two or more beetles, or once a plant has lost 25 percent of its leaves. Squash and pumpkins with four or more leaves tolerate feeding.

conventional: Treat only at the threshold, with a product labelled for cucumber beetles on that crop.

pests.signs: A velvety green caterpillar about 2.5 cm long, the young of the white cabbage butterfly. It chews holes in the leaves and pupates in a chrysalis on the plant.

cultural: Control weeds, and clear crop debris right after harvest so pests cannot finish their life cycle.
physical: Hand-pick caterpillars every few days on small plantings.
Cover plants with fine mesh netting to keep the butterflies from laying eggs.
biological: Grow small flowers such as sweet alyssum, parsley, dill, cilantro, buckwheat, and fennel, which draw parasitic flies and wasps.
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill these natural enemies.

regions.when: Every few days while the butterflies are flying, to catch caterpillars soon after they hatch.

organic: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad on active caterpillars, not on pupae.
conventional: Broad-spectrum insecticides such as carbaryl or bifenthrin, as a last resort.

pests.signs: Round brown spots up to 1.3 cm across with target-like rings, often ringed with yellow, starting on the oldest leaves near the ground. Leaves brown and drop. Seedling stems can rot dark and sunken at the soil line, and tomato fruit gets leathery black spots near the stem.

cultural: Grow resistant varieties, often marked EB in catalogues; they still show some spots.
Wait at least two years before growing tomatoes, potatoes, or peppers in the same place, and pull nightshade weeds.
Mulch under plants, water at the base, and stake, space, and prune the lowest leaves so leaves stay dry and soil does not splash onto them.
Use clean seed, and remove or bury plants at the end of the season.
physical: Remove spotted leaves, no more than a third of the plant, and wash hands and tools afterwards.

regions.when: Check the lower leaves regularly from early summer (mid to late June in Minnesota), more in warm wet weather with heavy dew; it spreads at 15 to 27 °C and most at 28 to 30 °C.
regions.threshold: Tomato plants tolerate a lot of early blight without losing yield; garden plants seldom need a fungicide.

conventional: Rarely needed in a garden. Where used, time fungicides to wet weather and rotate fungicide groups so resistance does not build.

regions.reference: UMN, "Early blight in tomato and potato" (reviewed 2024)

pests.signs: Large, dark brown blotches with a grey-green edge that cross the leaf veins, firm dark brown patches on stems, and in humid weather a thin white fuzz on infected parts. In cool wet weather whole plants turn brown as if frosted. Tomato fruit gets firm brown spots, and potato tubers discolour and rot.

cultural: Plant tomatoes where no tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, or eggplant have grown for three to four years.
Grow resistant varieties; they still show some symptoms in very wet years.
Plant certified seed potatoes, check transplants for spots, and pull volunteer potatoes.
Keep leaves dry with drip or soaker watering in the morning, and stake and space plants for air.
Remove or bury plants at the end of the season, and let potato culls break down over winter.
physical: Remove diseased leaves, and pull badly infected plants before it spreads.

regions.when: In cool (16 to 21 °C), damp weather; it does not come every year. Check tomato transplants before buying them, and look early in the day.

conventional: Not recommended in home gardens. Farms use fungicides made for water moulds, applied before infection and rotated.

pests.signs: Pale yellow leaf spots, then white powdery patches on both sides of the leaves that spread over leaves, stems, and leaf stalks, older leaves first. Plants weaken, fruit ripens early and gets sunscald, and it stores and tastes worse.

cultural: Grow varieties with full or partial resistance.
Space plants properly, stake them, and control weeds so air moves around them; avoid shady sites.
Fertilize by soil test, without extra nitrogen.

regions.when: From mid to late summer, once plants are fruiting; once a week, look at five mature leaves.
regions.threshold: Where fungicides are used, start when 1 of every 50 leaves checked has powdery mildew.

conventional: Only where susceptible varieties lost yield before; start when it first appears, and check current recommendations, as it keeps developing resistance.

pests.signs: Beetles 8 to 13 mm long with a metallic green head and copper-brown wing covers, and five tufts of white hair along each side and two at the tip. They eat the leaf between the veins, leaving a lacy skeleton that browns, and feed on flowers and fruit, often in clusters on one plant while its neighbours are spared. The C-shaped white grubs feed mainly on grass roots.

cultural: Harvest often while the beetles are feeding, which leaves them less of the crop.
physical: Hand-pick or knock beetles into soapy water every day, best in the cool of morning or evening; fewer damaged leaves draw fewer beetles.
Cover plants with fine netting, but only after flowering and fruit set, so pollinators can reach the flowers.
Do not hang beetle traps in a garden; they draw in more beetles than they catch.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Popillia japonica distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26); absent, transient, or only intercepted elsewhere

regions.when: Adults come out of the ground in late June or early July and feed for six to eight weeks, mostly finished by mid to late August. Start removing them as soon as the first appear.
regions.threshold: Damage to mature plants is mostly cosmetic; young or weak plants and fruit are worth protecting.

biological: Two natural enemies are established in Minnesota, the Winsome fly (Istocheta aldrichi) on adults and the wasp Tiphia vernalis on grubs. Leave any beetle with a white egg on its back; the fly laid it and will kill the beetle within a week.
organic: Neem oil deters feeding for a few days and is low risk to bees; repeat it.
Pyrethrins kill only beetles they hit and are toxic to bees.
conventional: Chlorantraniliprole protects for two to four weeks and is low risk to bees.
Pyrethroids (bifenthrin, cyfluthrin, lambda-cyhalothrin, permethrin) and carbaryl last longer but are toxic to bees and other pollinators.

pests.signs: A rounded beetle about 8 mm long, like a lady beetle, orange to copper with 16 black spots in three rows. Clusters of 40 to 60 bright yellow eggs stand on end under the leaves, and the yellow larvae are covered in soft black spines. Larvae and adults eat the underside of leaves between the veins, leaving them lacy and see-through; adults also feed on flowers, pods, and stems.

cultural: Sow a small patch of beans early in spring as a trap; once overwintered adults have gathered on it, pull the plants into sealed bags to destroy them.
Pull and bag bean plants after harvest, which kills the eggs, larvae, and pupae on them.
physical: Cover bean rows with row cover after sowing; it can stay on until harvest, as beans need no pollinators.
Crush egg clusters, larvae, and adults by hand, and seal badly infested plants in a plastic bag for a week before composting them.
biological: Release the parasitic wasp Pediobius faveolatus when the first larvae appear; it suits large plantings and community gardens.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Epilachna varivestis distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: From early summer, look under the leaves for yellow egg clusters; there are one to three generations a year.
regions.threshold: Beans tolerate the loss of up to 20 percent of their leaves before yield drops.

organic: For severe infestations, spinosad, neem, or pyrethrum.

regions.reference: University of Maryland Extension HGIC, "Mexican bean beetle" (updated 2023)

pests.signs: Tiny yellow-orange mites, about 0.5 mm long, with a dark spot on each side, under the leaves. Feeding leaves fine white or yellow speckles, then a bronzed or bleached look, and leaves can drop; heavy infestations spin fine webbing over the leaves. It can be mistaken for drought stress.

cultural: Keep plants watered (about 2.5 cm a week) and mulched; mites thrive on stressed plants. Do not fertilize during drought.
physical: Knock mites off with a strong spray of water, which also breaks up their webbing.
biological: Predatory mites and the small lady beetles that eat mites keep numbers down; long-lasting insecticides such as bifenthrin and permethrin kill them and can make mites worse.

regions.when: Every three to five days in hot, dry summer weather, looking under speckled leaves with a hand lens, or tapping leaves over white paper and watching for moving specks. Above 32 °C colonies can build up in under two weeks.

organic: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil kill only the mites they touch and have little effect on other insects; spray both sides of the leaves, repeat, and water plants first and spray in the cool of morning or evening.

pests.signs: A green caterpillar 3 to 4 cm long, wider at the tail than the head, that walks in loops like an inchworm and rears up when disturbed; it has only two pairs of fleshy legs on its abdomen, where other cabbage caterpillars have four. It chews large holes in the leaves and pupates in a loose cocoon under a leaf.

cultural: Control weeds, and clear crop debris right after harvest so pests cannot finish their life cycle.
physical: Hand-pick caterpillars every few days on small plantings.
Cover plants with fine mesh netting to keep the moths from laying eggs.
biological: Grow small flowers such as sweet alyssum, parsley, dill, cilantro, buckwheat, and fennel, which draw parasitic flies and wasps.
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill these natural enemies.

regions.when: Every few days, to catch caterpillars soon after they hatch.

organic: Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad on active caterpillars, not on pupae.
conventional: Broad-spectrum insecticides such as carbaryl or bifenthrin, as a last resort.

pests.signs: Small, round grey spots with dark borders on the lower leaves, with tiny black specks (the fungus's fruiting bodies) in their centres. The spots grow together, and leaves yellow and die from the bottom of the plant up.

cultural: Space plants for air, remove suckers from the base, and prune off the lowest three or four leaf branches once plants are setting fruit.
Mulch, and water at the base so the leaves stay dry.
Check transplants for spots before planting them, and pull horsenettle, a weed host.
Remove infected leaves during the season and all infected plant parts at its end; hot composting above 49 °C kills it.

regions.when: Spots usually appear as the first fruit forms, and spread in wet weather.

organic: Where it blights plants badly every year, fixed copper, early in the season when spots first appear.
conventional: A synthetic fungicide, at the same time and only in the same case.

regions.reference: University of Maryland Extension HGIC, "Septoria leaf spot on tomatoes" (updated 2024)

regions.when: In seasons of moderate temperatures and plenty of rain; rain splash spreads it, so look after wet spells.

cultural: Rotate away from tomatoes for two years or more, and avoid working among wet plants.
organic: Fixed copper.
conventional: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb.

regions.reference: NC State Extension, "Septoria leaf spot of tomato" (I. Meadows and T. Clabby)

pests.signs: Leaves turn dull green and wilt in the heat of the day, recover overnight at first, then yellow and brown from the edges and die as the wilt moves down the vine. Cucumbers and melons collapse fast, pumpkins over about two weeks, and summer squash may keep bearing for weeks. Cutting a wilted stem near the crown and slowly pulling the halves apart can show fine strands of ooze. Cucumber beetles carry it; it does not affect watermelon.

cultural: Control cucumber beetles, which carry the bacteria from plant to plant; it is the most effective protection.
Pull and bury plants that wilt from it, before beetles spread it further.
Grow resistant varieties where catalogues offer them.
Rule out squash vine borer at the crown, and drought, before blaming wilt.
physical: Cover young plants with row cover from emergence, and remove it at flowering so pollinators can reach the flowers.

regions.when: Watch for plants that wilt in the afternoon and have not recovered by morning; it does not appear every year.
regions.threshold: No spray cures an infected plant; any insecticide is aimed at the cucumber beetles that spread it.

pests.signs: Round, velvety, olive-green spots up to 1.3 cm across with fringed edges, often along the leaf veins, that turn dark brown to black and run together. Badly spotted leaves yellow and drop by midsummer. Fruit gets olive spots that turn brown and corky, and fruit infected young cracks and misshapes. Years of early leaf loss weaken the tree.

cultural: Plant resistant or immune varieties; it is the best defence.
Rake up and destroy, bury, or compost fallen leaves before snow, or chop them with a mulching mower, as the fungus spends the winter in them.
Space trees by their mature size and prune for an open canopy, removing suckers and water sprouts, so leaves dry quickly.

regions.when: Spores fly in spring and infect new leaves, flowers, and fruit whenever they stay wet for several hours; warm, rainy springs are worst. In mid-June, check leaves inside and outside the canopy for spots.
regions.threshold: Spray only trees whose fruit is for eating fresh and that have had severe scab before, or trees that lost most of their leaves three years running; not resistant varieties, and not a tree already spotted this year, since fungicides only protect.

cultural: Resistant in Minnesota trials, Honeycrisp; immune, Dayton, Freedom, Liberty, McShay, Pixie Crunch, Pristine, Redfree, and William's Pride.
organic: For edible apples, lime-sulfur or sulfur, from when half an inch of green leaf shows at bud break, repeated at the label's interval, shorter in rainy weather.
conventional: Captan, at the same times; do not follow captan closely with lime-sulfur.
Never use an all-purpose fruit spray during bloom; its insecticide kills pollinators.

pests.signs: A shield-shaped, mottled brown bug with alternating light and dark bands on its antennae and along the edge of its abdomen, which tell it from native stink bugs; it smells when crushed. It lays clusters of barrel-shaped eggs on leaves, and young nymphs have a yellow-red abdomen. Feeding on developing fruit leaves misshapen, discoloured patches.

physical: Pick or shake bugs into soapy water.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Halyomorpha halys distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: Adults come out in May and numbers peak from mid-August through October, when they gather on buildings to spend the winter indoors.
regions.threshold: No garden damage has been reported in Minnesota, so no management aimed at it is needed there; it is a major pest of these crops in other states.

pests.signs: A small fruit fly, 2 to 3 mm, yellowish-brown with red eyes; the male has a dark spot near each wingtip. Unlike other fruit flies it lays eggs in sound, ripening fruit, and tiny white maggots feed inside, leaving soft, sunken, sour-smelling berries, sometimes only after picking. Healthy apples, pears, and cherry tomatoes are not attacked.

cultural: Pick often so ripe fruit does not linger, and remove old and fallen fruit.
Seal infested fruit in a plastic bag for the sun or the trash; do not compost or bury it, as the flies survive both.
Chill picked fruit to slow any larvae inside; it is safe to eat.
physical: Cover plants with fine insect netting (80-gram) or a small tunnel; coarser netting lets the flies through. Raspberries still set fruit under it.
Hang vinegar traps (a cup with small holes and a little cider vinegar) near the fruit from fruit set to the end of harvest, and check them weekly, to know when flies are active.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Drosophila suzukii distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: Flies appear in late June or early July and peak in August and September; watch most closely from when fruit starts to colour until harvest.

organic: Spinosad or pyrethrin, both allowed in organic growing. They kill adults before they lay eggs, not larvae already in fruit; spray in the evening to spare pollinators, and rotate classes, as it can develop resistance.
conventional: Carbaryl or malathion, with the same timing.

pests.signs: Slender, yellow-brown insects about 1.5 mm long with fringed wings, hiding deep in the neck of onion plants among the youngest leaves. Feeding leaves white to silver patches and streaks, heavy feeding stunts the bulbs, and thrips spread iris yellow spot virus, which makes straw-coloured, diamond-shaped spots on onion leaves.

cultural: Check onion transplants and discard any carrying thrips.
Feed enough nitrogen but not too much, and mulch beds with straw.
Grow carrots among onions, which draws thrips away from them.
Overhead watering washes thrips off and slows them.
Remove volunteer onions and onion debris before planting and after harvest.
Varieties with an open neck and dark, glossy leaves draw fewer thrips; red onions suffer most.
biological: Predators build up by late summer where broad-spectrum insecticides are not used.

regions.when: From when plants have four or five leaves, or mid-June; open the neck and count the thrips at the base of the youngest leaves. Bulb swelling, in July and early August, is when they do most harm.
regions.threshold: About 15 thrips per plant in early summer or on red onions; about 30 per plant in July and August on tolerant yellow and white onions.

conventional: Thrips quickly resist insecticides; spray as few times as possible, rotate insecticide classes, and drive the spray into the neck where they hide.

regions.reference: Utah State University Extension, "Onion thrips" fact sheet (D. Alston and D. Drost, 2008)

pests.signs: The pinkish-white "worm" in the apple, with a dark brown head. It bores into fruit soon after hatching and tunnels to the core, leaving entry holes plugged with reddish-brown, crumbly droppings. The grey moth, 1.3 to 2 cm, holds its wings like a tent and has a coppery band at the wingtips.

cultural: Choose early-maturing varieties, which suffer less, and keep trees low enough to reach the fruit.
Every week or two from six to eight weeks after bloom, remove fruit with frass-filled holes, and pick up dropped fruit at once.
physical: Four to six weeks after bloom, when fruit is 1.3 to 2.5 cm across, thin to one fruit per cluster and enclose each in a paper lunch bag slit at the bottom and stapled shut; this alone protects fruit even in bad years.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Cydia pomonella distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: Moths emerge from mid-March to April and mate once sunset temperatures pass 17 °C; two to four generations follow. Hang a pheromone trap in March and check it every few days; eggs hatch about 250 to 300 degree-days (°F) after the first moths are caught.

organic: Time every spray to egg hatch, by degree-days or the first fresh entry holes; sprays miss larvae already inside fruit.
Codling moth granulosis virus, with 1 percent horticultural oil, every 7 days, three or four times a generation; it spares bees and beneficial insects.
Spinosad with 1 percent horticultural oil, every 10 days, about three times a generation.

regions.reference: UC IPM, "Codling moth" Pest Notes and Quick Tips (Home and Landscape)

pests.signs: A dark brown snout beetle about 5 mm long, its snout a third as long as its body, with four bumps and grey-white patches on its back. Females cut small crescent scars in young fruit to lay eggs; the legless, curved white grubs feed inside, and infested apples drop with the June drop. Egg scars stay on fruit that does not fall.

physical: Repeated coats of kaolin clay protect fruit, and organic growers rely on it.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Conotrachelus nenuphar distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: From bloom until about two weeks after petal fall, check the outer trees for fresh feeding and egg scars; attacks on apple start once fruit is about 6 mm across.

conventional: Usually two or three sprays aimed at the beetle, timed by the current regional tree fruit guide.

regions.reference: University of New Hampshire Extension, "Plum curculio" fact sheet (A. T. Eaton)

pests.signs: Stiff white maggots about 8 mm long tunnel just under the skin of carrot roots, leaving tunnels filled with rusty mush. Nothing shows above ground.

cultural: Harvest as soon as roots are ready, a whole block at a time rather than a few, and do not leave carrots in the ground over winter.
Remove parsley, celery, and related plants that harbour it, and peel off damaged parts before eating.
physical: Cover seedbeds with row cover, or single plants with protective cones.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Chamaepsila rosae (its accepted name) distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: Check roots as you harvest; there is no sign above ground.

cultural: Sow to miss the fly's egg-laying, in early summer in cold areas and in late winter or late summer in mild ones.

regions.reference: UC IPM, "Carrot rust fly" (Home and Landscape)

pests.signs: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper side of leaves, angular because the veins bound them (clearest on cucumber), with dark purplish-grey fuzz underneath in humid weather. The spots brown and run together until leaves look frost-killed; watermelon leaves curl upward. Angular leaf spot and powdery mildew can look similar.

cultural: Grow resistant varieties where you have had it before; cucumbers have the best resistance, melons less.
Water by drip, space rows widely, and trellis plants so leaves dry quickly.
Remove plants with symptoms.

regions.when: It does not survive Minnesota winters and arrives on winds from the south, in many years not at all, and often not before August. It spreads fastest at 15 to 20 °C with wet leaves.
regions.threshold: No product that works against it is available to home gardeners.

pests.signs: Young shoots wilt, turn grey-green, and bend into a shepherd's hook, then blacken, so the tree looks scorched; the dead leaves cling into winter. Blossoms turn water-soaked and then brown or black, fruit shrivels into mummies, and sunken, cracked cankers on branches ooze cream to yellow droplets in humid weather. It can kill young trees.

cultural: Plant resistant varieties; none is immune, but resistant ones slow it enough to prune it out.

During the season, cut out infected shoots at least 30 cm below the infection; cut larger branches in late winter, at least 20 cm below the canker into healthy wood, and disinfect tools if a cut may have touched diseased wood.
Avoid heavy pruning and too much nitrogen, which push the soft new growth it infects; fertilize by soil test.

occursIn.reference: EPPO (2026), EPPO Global Database, Erwinia amylovora distribution, countries where present (accessed 2026-11-26)

regions.when: In warm (above 18 °C), humid or rainy spells in spring and summer; blossom infection is less common in Minnesota, where it is usually cool at bloom.

cultural: Most resistant of the apples hardy in Minnesota, Haralson, Liberty, Red Baron, SnowSweet, and the Chestnut and Dolgo crabs; Honeycrisp and Zestar! are somewhat resistant.
